extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, formal-verification researchers, and mathematicians interested in proof assistants and foundations
extracted.subtask_description: An analytic overview of what it takes to understand, represent, and evaluate mathematical language, proofs, concepts, and diagrammatic reasoning—with attention to how interactive theorem proving (formal verification) models and informs those notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical value judgments (interestingness, importance, explanatory power, conceptual power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice routinely issues normative evaluations beyond correctness: questions can be interesting or natural; theorems important; proofs explanatory; concepts powerful or fruitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the sorts of judgments traditionally grouped under 'mathematical understanding' and they shape research, pedagogy, and support. The essay treats such evaluations as substantive phenomena to be analyzed rather than mere aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mathematical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding mathematical language, involves, in part, being able to identify the fundamental logical and mathematical structure of an assertion, that is, recognize logical connectives and quantifiers, function application, predication, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal-verification work models this via frameworks (ZF, simple type theory, dependent/type theories). Examples: HOL light encoding of the Jordan curve theorem; Kieffer's rendering of Munkres definitions and natural-language rendering. Competence includes parsing notation, scope of quantifiers, and mapping symbols to intended domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mathematical proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding mathematical proof involves, in part, being able to recognize contextual cues, explicit or implicit reliance on local assumptions, background knowledge, recently established facts, and so on; and to determine whether inferences are a matter of calculation, unwrapping definitions, applying a lemma, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs are higher-level descriptions or 'recipes' for low-level formal derivations. Formal proof languages (Isabelle/Isar, Mizar, Ssreflect/Coq) expose different desiderata: readability, explicit intermediate goals, compactness. Good proof representation should make context, case-splits, and uses of lemmas apparent; examples: Isabelle proof script vs Isar readable proof; Ssreflect compact lines combining many small steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mathematical domains and structures (types, coercions, overloading, polymorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding mathematical conventions regarding domains and types involves being able to resolve ambiguities and infer type information from the context; being able to recognize concrete domains as implicitly embedded in other domains; being able to recognize concrete and abstract structures as instances of more general classes of structures; and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal systems must support type inference, overloading, coercions, polymorphism, and implicit arguments so that expressions like summations, products, or embeddings (integers→reals→complex) can be treated smoothly. The essay gives many examples (summation in various monoids, viewing a field as vector space over a subfield) and notes that automated insertion of coercions/implicit args via unification is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mathematical inference (decision vs search, domain-general vs domain-specific, principled vs heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding mathematics involves being able to carry out straightforward mathematical inferences in specific mathematical domains, even when those inferences are difficult to spell out in formal axiomatic terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated reasoning divides into decision procedures (guaranteed termination) and search procedures (may not halt), domain-general and domain-specific methods, and principled vs heuristic approaches. Strengths: large homogeneous calculations. Weaknesses: chaining heterogeneous background knowledge. The rubric values the ability to perform 'straightforward' inferences that might be informal but are cognitively natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding diagrammatic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrammatic reasoning is a genuine component of mathematical reasoning: diagrams can guide proofs, make arguments intelligible, and sometimes be convincing on their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although modern professional texts minimize diagrams, the essay argues for taking diagrammatic inferences seriously (Euclidean geometry examples) and for formal systems or analyses that can account for the normative rules governing diagram use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of multiple proofs (proofs provide more than warrant of truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new proof of an already-established theorem can be highly valued because it 'shows a new connection' or provides new insights and understanding beyond merely establishing truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should account for explanatory content, new conceptual relations, methodological import, or opening avenues for generalization—e.g., Furstenberg's ergodic proof of Szemerédi's theorem spawning ergodic Ramsey theory. The criterion asks whether a proof contributes understanding, new connections, or conceptual tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of conceptual possibility (concepts enabling proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical advances are often said to have been 'made possible' by prior conceptual developments (new definitions, concepts, or frameworks); explaining this 'possibility' requires modeling why producing good definitions can be difficult and why they enable new proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment includes whether conceptual innovations render previously inaccessible results tractable, and whether the framework supports natural formulations and derivations (historical examples: Riemann's zeta function enabling analytic proofs of the prime number theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal-modeling desiderata for proof assistants (language & inference robustness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive theorem proving requires underlying formal frameworks that specify assertion languages and admissible inference rules; these frameworks must robustly model typing, definition mechanisms, and inference patterns found in ordinary mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: choice of ZF (Mizar) vs simple-type HOL (HOL/HOL Light/Isabelle) vs dependent/type theories (Coq). Considerations include expressiveness, convenience for mathematics, and support for extracting formal proof objects. Projects (four-color, prime number theorem, Jordan curve, Feit-Thompson, Kepler) illustrate the kind of large-scale verification envisioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-language/readability tradeoffs (script efficiency vs human readability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different proof languages balance compact, efficient scripting against explicit, human-readable structure; understanding and evaluating proofs includes assessing whether a representation makes goals and contexts sufficiently explicit for human understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isabelle proof scripts are terse and operate by replaying tactics; Isar/Mizar styles make intermediate goals explicit; Ssreflect/Coq is compact and efficient but dense. Evaluations may consider maintainability, ease of replaying, and the ability to convey explanatory structure, not just formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple views and implicit embeddings of objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Competence requires recognizing when the same mathematical object can legitimately be viewed in multiple ways (e.g., a field as a vector space, subsets closed under operations as subgroups) and reliably switching or coercing between views in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal systems need mechanisms (coercions, canonical structures/type classes) to support such multiple views; human judgments rely on recognizing which view is operative and what properties can be used. Examples: intersections of subgroups as groups; interpreting summation operator in various algebraic settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity, ease, and difficulty as normative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of complexity and diﬃculty (proof length, computational complexity, cognitive cost) play a role in judging mathematical value: good definitions and methods reduce complexity, simplify tasks, and thus have normative force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay critiques naive measures (formal proof length, asymptotic complexity, raw psychological measures) and calls for measures tailored to pragmatic mathematical use—ones that account for cognitive constraints, typical problem sizes, and the ways conceptual choices streamline ordinary mathematical practice (e.g., proof mining, proof-complexity speedups, but with caution about overinterpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normativity and objectivity of mathematical values
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments about naturalness, explanatory power, and appropriate representations are reasoned and can be objective insofar as they extend the capacities of agents with cognitive constraints similar to ours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion concerns whether value judgments can be grounded: provide idealizations of cognitive capacities to show that certain representations or methods systematically extend reasoning ability. This is a methodological demand on philosophical accounts of mathematical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of automated reasoning tools and domain-specific procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective mathematical understanding (in practice and in formalization) requires integrating automated reasoning tools—decision procedures, domain-specific solvers, and computer-algebra techniques—where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: linear-arithmetic solvers, real-closed-field fragments, Gröbner-basis methods; combining domain-specific methods into general proof-search frameworks (Nelson–Oppen style) is important. The rubric values judicious use of automation to fill routine gaps while preserving explanatory structure.
